opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the hardest and most underrated problems in the whole pipeline. People tend to imagine that the bottleneck in formalization is the Lean proof itself, the tactic-level work. In practice, a lot of the difficulty sits one level up: going from a human-written paper to a blueprint that is detailed enough to be formalized at all.

A typical arXiv paper is written for experts. It skips steps that the author considers routine. It says "by a standard argument" or "it is easy to see," and it relies on a huge amount of background knowledge. It may silently use a slightly different definition than the one in the literature, or one that doesn't exist yet in Mathlib. So the first challenge is really an unfolding problem. You have to recover all of those implicit steps and make every dependency explicit.

Then there's the structural challenge. A good blueprint isn't just a longer version of the paper. It's a dependency graph: definitions, lemmas, and theorems, each stated precisely enough that a human or a machine can go formalize that one node without having to understand the whole paper. Deciding how to decompose the argument, what the right intermediate lemmas are, and which statements are at the right granularity is a real mathematical skill. Experienced formalizers spend a lot of time on exactly that.

The third piece is alignment with the existing library. You need to know what's already in Mathlib, what's almost there, and what has to be built from scratch, and you need to state things in a way that fits the library's conventions. Otherwise you end up with a blueprint that looks fine on paper but is painful to actually formalize.

So for a computer, it requires a combination of things: deep mathematical understanding to fill in the gaps correctly, good judgment about decomposition, and fluency with the formal ecosystem. Language models have gotten quite good at the first kind of reading. They can often explain what a paper is doing. But producing something that is faithful, complete, and formalization-ready is a much stricter bar, because any small mistake or hidden gap shows up later when you try to compile.

The nice thing is that the problem has a built-in verifier downstream. If the blueprint is wrong or underspecified, Lean will eventually tell you. That feedback loop is what makes me optimistic. It's hard, but it's the kind of hard where you can measure progress, and that's exactly the kind of problem where AI tends to improve quickly.

r001.rationale: The response calls the task “one of the hardest” problems and explains that producing a blueprint detailed enough for formalization requires making implicit steps explicit and decomposing the argument precisely.

fable-5.1.text:
It's much harder than it looks from the outside, and the reason is that a math paper is not actually a proof. It's a compressed set of hints written for a reader who already shares the author's intuition. When a paper says "by a standard compactness argument" or "it follows easily from Lemma 3.2," a human expert fills in two pages in their head. The computer has to produce those two pages explicitly, and often it has to first figure out which two pages the author meant.

So when we talk about going from an arXiv paper to a blueprint, there are really three layers of difficulty. The first is just understanding the dependency structure: which statements rely on which, what's really the load-bearing lemma, what's a remark that can be skipped. That part is becoming tractable for language models, honestly. The second layer is translating informal statements into precise Lean statements, and this is where a lot of subtlety hides. A paper will write "let G be a group" and later quietly assume it's finite, or use a definition that's slightly different from the one in Mathlib. Getting the statement wrong means you might formalize something true but not what the paper claims, or something that's unprovable. The third layer is the actual gap-filling, where every "clearly" becomes a real obligation.

What I've found is that the blueprint stage is where most of the intellectual work actually concentrates. If you get a good blueprint, meaning every node is a precise statement with a clear set of dependencies and the gaps are small enough, then proving the individual pieces is increasingly something automation can handle. But producing that blueprint requires taste. You have to decide how to decompose things, what level of generality to work at, whether to prove something directly or via a more abstract route that already exists in the library.

I'd say today a system can produce a plausible-looking blueprint for a lot of papers, but plausible-looking and correct are different things. The failure mode is confident mistranslation. And the interesting part is that fixing this isn't just about more compute. It's about building systems that can check their own understanding against the library and against the paper, and that know when to ask a human.

r001.rationale: The response calls the task “much harder than it looks” and explains that producing a correct, precise blueprint requires resolving dependencies, translating statements into Lean, and filling proof gaps.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite difficult, because a detailed blueprint has to do much more than summarize the paper. It needs to identify the precise definitions, break the argument into intermediate lemmas, and make clear which results depend on which others. A mathematician might read a sentence like “this follows by a standard argument” and fill in the gap. For formalization, that gap can represent a substantial amount of work.

There’s also the question of what already exists in Lean. A proof might be straightforward on paper, but if the underlying machinery hasn’t been formalized, you may need to build that first. So a useful blueprint needs to connect the mathematical argument to the available library.

I’d distinguish between producing a plausible outline and producing a blueprint that someone can actually follow to complete the formalization. The first seems much more accessible. The second requires checking details, and probably an iterative process where attempts at formalization reveal what the blueprint is missing.

r001.rationale: The response calls the task “quite difficult,” but does not clearly characterize it as extremely difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very difficult, because a mathematics paper and a Lean proof operate at quite different levels of detail. In a paper, an author might say, “By a standard argument,” and that could hide a substantial amount of work. A blueprint has to unpack that argument: what are the precise statements, which intermediate lemmas do we need, and how do they depend on one another?

And then there’s the question of what already exists in Lean. Something that looks like one step on paper might require building a whole missing piece of the library. So the computer needs both mathematical understanding and an understanding of the formal environment.

Producing a plausible outline is one thing. Producing a detailed blueprint that actually makes the formalization easier is a much higher bar. The useful test is whether someone can follow it and make the proof go through.

r001.rationale: The response says it is “very difficult” for a computer to produce a detailed blueprint and explains that it must unpack arguments into precise statements, lemmas, and dependencies while accounting for Lean’s existing library.
